text: you are railing against a game which in your view is "excluding" beginners. that's gatekeeping too to the degree the solution is to exclude more experienced gamers, which in a lot of cases it is. a souls game that caters to beginners wouldn't be a souls game so now you are excluding people who prefer a challenge and no handholding in their game, and also enjoy the kind of shared competition miyazaki intended when he claimed he wants everybody to have the same "experience", so no easy mode is intended by the designer and is an integral element of the game (in my opinion you cannot actually have an easy mode in souls because difficutly in those games has nothing to do with fudging numbers. you would have to redesign the whole game from the ground up for each difficutly setting, have alternative boss patterns for each etc it would be a massive endeavour with no pay off). as for bullet hell games, this is a genre of game that is designed specifically to be impossibly hard. it's their entire reason for being, so they are exclutionary by their very nature, that's why i asked whether they ought to be allowed to exist as a genre. you can see this whenever they include easy modalities, which serve no purpose since those games do not offer much value besides the gameplay challenge and competition through the scording mechanic is also nullified in those easy modalities. if you strip that out of the game all you have is a colored light show that barely lasts 30 minutes, hardly enough to ask people to pay for that. ultimately, this entire argument boils down to two points. first, whether there is anything wrong with "excluding" certain people, which in my view there isn't (gatekeeping isn't necessarely a bad thing, it just depends). second, whether the inclusion of less skilled players comes at the expense of the exclution of more hardcore oriented people, which in a lot of cases it does. there's also this sense you are claiming there is some kind of greater virtue to being a casual who just "wants to have fun" (emtional argument), but as an hardcore player, i want to have fun too and i don't see exactly why my priorities are less valuable than that of a casual player, except i guess there's more of them than me but now you are arguing for the superior rights of quantity and the lowest common denominator. of course, there's a simple solution to this, which is to make different games that are intended for different people. to me it really seems the problem for you is that you just want all games to be available to all people all at once, which is the case for most games already but in some cases it simply cannot happen. you cannot make a competitive multiplayer game "for the casuals". it is fundamentally impossible. some games will invariably have to exclude some people. in fact, now that i think about it, i personally think there is greater virtue to rising yourself to a particular challenge and elevate and improve yourself in the process than to just "have fun" while making no personal progress of any kind. that's probably what ticks me off about this whole conversation (which i had with other people already). the whole question for a "beginner" for me boils down to the ways a game can turn that beginner into a competent player. i do not particularly like this idea that beginners are intended to remain as such. i actually consider that to be a disservice to them as much as the medium. look at all the modern aaa slop with their braindead gameplay that literally plays itself, that stupid yellow paint etc. the whole design of a lot of modern games seems to be based on the idea novices have no desire nor any capability to grow as players. and to return to the origin of this entire argument, it's funny because that assumption on the part of game developers is the reason why a game like bg3 (isometic, turn based etc) was deemed non-viable for the modern market because such games are just too difficult for the "average", casual player. but lo and behold, the game was an hit, much like elden ring was a massive success too which seems to put that notion to rest. seems like casual players aren't so inept or incapable to rise up to challenges after all.
